## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta* (DN 9) is a major discourse in the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* of the *Dīghanikāya*. Set in Sāvatthi, the sutta begins when the Buddha visits the wanderer (*paribbājaka*) Poṭṭhapāda, who is seated among his followers engaged in worldly conversation, opening with a narrative formula shared with the *Udumbarika-sīhanāda Sutta* [Allon 1997; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. Like other suttas in this section of the *Dīghanikāya*, the text incorporates the extensive stock account of moral restraint and sense restraint drawn from the *Sāmaññaphala* scheme [Peoples 2013; Holder 2006; Polak 2011].

The central philosophical dialogue addresses the nature of perception (*saññā*) and the question of self (*attā*) [Holder 2006]. The Buddha describes the gradual training through the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the formless dimensions (*ārūpya-dhātu*), showing that perception arises and ceases through training rather than being identical to a permanent soul or self [Lusthaus 2002; Polak 2011; Jayatilleke 1963]. He refutes theories asserting three distinct acquisitions of self—gross, mind-made, and formless—explaining through the simile of milk, curds, butter, and ghee that such designations are merely conventional worldly terms (*saṅkhaṁ gacchati*) without metaphysical enduring entities [Jayatilleke 1963]. When questioned regarding the ten indeterminate (*avyākatāni*) metaphysical problems, the Buddha sets them aside as not leading to detachment or nibbāna [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Anderson 1999]. Following the dialogue, Poṭṭhapāda becomes a lay disciple, while his companion Citta Hatthisāriputta later joins the Sangha and achieves arahantship [Holder 2006; Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Anderson 1999].

Curated parallels include DĀ 28 in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* and Sanskrit fragments (SF 297, SF 59), alongside extensive internal parallels across the Nikāyas for its moral sections and meditation formulas. DharmaNexus aligns DN 9 with Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T1), *Madhyamāgama* (T26), and *Saṁyuktāgama* (T99), as well as Tibetan canonical texts and Sanskrit works including the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and Prajñāpāramitā literature [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records widespread text reuse, particularly with AN 10, the *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13), the *Udumbarika Sutta* (DN 25), the *Abyākata Saṁyutta* (SN 44), and its commentary in the *Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
